text: In The essay on Pico's philosophy of religion, De ente et uno is presented as reconciling the Aristotelian identity of the One and Being with the Platonist priority of the One over Being, which matters for Pico's account of God.

quotes.text: In his De ente et uno (1491), the reconciliation of Aristotelianism and Platonism proves essential to Pico’s reflections on the nature of God, specifically his unpacking the wholly transcendent and sui generis nature of God as the pure, unlimited act of existence. Pico sets out to reconcile the Aristotelian claim that the One and Being are the same and the Platonist contention that the One is prior to Being.

text: The essay reports that Pico distinguishes two senses of being, and that Aristotle, in identifying Being and the One, was using being in the sense of what is outside nothing, so that Aristotle's view is compatible with the Platonist one.

quotes.text: term being can be taken in two senses. According to the first, being signifies “all that which is outside nothing.” That which is nonbeing is nothing. According to the second, being signifies that which participates in existence (esse). Pico argues that when Aristotle identified Being and the One, he assumed Being in the former sense. He did not intend to assert that the One participates in Being, as, for example, luminosity participates in light. Hence, Aristotle’s view is compatible with the view advocated among Platonists.

warrants.text: The essay cites Pico's own words on God as the plenitude of existence (note 20, On Being and the One, p. 44).

quote.text: For God, who is the plentitude of all existence, is of this nature. He alone is of himself, and from him alone, with no interposing medium, all things proceed to existence.

judged.justification: Concise statement of how the concord works: two senses of 'being', so that the Aristotelian identity does not put the One under Being.

text: The essay reads Pico's view of God as the plenitude of existence as reproducing the Thomistic position that God is the act of existence itself.

quotes.text: Pico’s view here reproduces the Thomistic position that God is ipsum esse, the act of existence of itself.

warrants.text: Sudduth's note 21 points to the Summa theologiae of Aquinas (Ia, q. 4, a. 2, corp.).

text: The essay reports Pico's three worlds, the first being the angelic realm for theologians and the intelligible realm for Platonists, and says Pico adds the human person as a fourth.

quotes.text: Pico distinguished between the ultramundane, celestial, and sublunary worlds. The last world is the one inhabited by all living things on earth. The first is the angelic realm (as described by theologians) or the intelligible realm (as described by Platonists). The celestial world is the realm above the earth, embracing the stars and planets, but below the ultramundane world. To these three worlds, Pico adds a fourth: the human person.

warrants.text: The essay quotes Heptaplus (second proem) on the containment of all things in each world.

quote.text: whatever is in any of the worlds is contained in each.

text: The essay argues that the mutual containment of the worlds is the metaphysical basis of Pico's method of allegorical interpretation, because discourse about one level must refer to others.

quotes.text: Pico is explicit that the basis for his method of allegorical interpretation is a metaphysical principle of the mutual containment of all levels of reality
It is because all things are contained in each other that discourse about any one level of reality is bound to involve reference to other levels of reality.

warrants.text: The essay quotes Pico's Heptaplus for the exchange of natures and names among the worlds.

quote.text: Bound by chains of concord, all these worlds exchange natures as well as names with mutual liberality.

judged.justification: Ties the doctrine of the worlds (and so of the angelic world) to hermeneutic method.

text: The essay argues that Pico keeps the medieval chain of being but departs from it in one respect: the human person's ontological status is not fixed, between the angelic and animal worlds, but open to ascent or descent.

quotes.text: The human person was created “a little lower than the angels,” to quote the Psalmist. While retaining much of this general medieval metaphysics, Pico’s departs from it in a crucial respect. The ontological status of the human person is not fixed.

warrants.text: The essay quotes the Oration's speech of God to Adam.

quote.text: Thou canst grow downward into the lower natures which are brutes. Thou canst again grow upward from thy soul’s reason into higher natures which are divine.

text: In a note the essay reports the Florentine Neoplatonists, Ficino among them, as placing the human soul in the middle of the chain of being, capable of descending or ascending by free will.

quotes.text: The idea had been emphasized in the metaphysics of the Platonist Academy at Florence where Pico spent time studying. Neoplatonists such as Marsilio Ficino placed the “human soul” in the middle of the Great Chain of Being: Body → Quality → Soul → Angel → God.

bears_on.note: The essay treats the Florentine Academy and Ficino as the background of Pico's idea of the human soul between angel and body

text: The essay argues that for Pico the multiplicity of perspectives derives from the emanation of the One through a succession of intermediaries, and truth is finally one.

quotes.text: emanation of the One, God, through a succession of intermediaries. Perspectival multiplicity is thus grounded in both human freedom and the larger ontological structure of things. But behind it all is the perspective of the One.
In Pico’s Neoplatonist cosmological scheme, all things ultimately return to the One.

text: The essay says Pico, following the Platonists, sets an intellectual and angelic part of the human soul above the rational soul, unlike the Latin Aristotelians who take the rational part to be the highest.

quotes.text: Strictly speaking, the differentiation of the intellectual from the rational as distinct powers of soul is anomalous in scholastic terms, since, as Pico notes in his early Commento, “Latin Aristotelians” take the rational part “to be the highest and noblest part of our soul.”

While the Latin scholastics recognized that the rational soul contained within it the power of purely intellectual thought associated with the angels, Pico follows the Platonists, for whom there is an “intellectual and angelic part” of the human soul above the rational soul.

warrants.text: Note 12 names Plotinus's Enneads and Ficino's De amore as the proximate Platonic sources.

quote.text: The most proximate Platonic source is Plotinus Enneads IV.2.2; see also Ficino De amore VI.13.

bears_on.note: the essay's note points to Ficino's De amore alongside Plotinus as source for the angelic part of the soul

judged.justification: Locates the angelic element inside the human soul rather than only above it.

text: The essay's note suggests that in placing an angelic part in the soul Pico is implying that angelic cognition, immediate knowing without reasoning, lies within the natural capacity of the human mind.

quotes.text: While Pico would not regard the soul as literally divided into parts, he is suggesting that angelic cognition – immediate knowing without reasoning – lies within the natural capacity of the human mind.

text: The essay reports the Thomist view that a human knower in this life has no direct cognition of any spiritual being, so humans can only approximate the angelic mode of knowing in rare moments of immediate intuition.

quotes.text: For Aquinas, this had meant that there could be no direct cognition or “vision” of God or any spiritual being by a human knower while still in this life, which is to say by virtue of natural human powers.

Human beings, then, unable ever to become purely spiritual intelligences, can only approximate the angelic mode of knowing in rare moments of immediate intellectual intuition, as when grasping first principles or intuiting the essence of a perceived object.

text: The essay says the Heptaplus gives a fivefold account of human nature, the fifth part being an intelligence shared with the angels.

quotes.text: In the course of his allegorized interpretation of Genesis 1 there, Pico lays out a similar yet slightly more nuanced schema of human nature, featuring five parts: (1) the rational soul; (2) the mortal body; (3) an “intervening spirit,” which serves as a “connecting link” between soul and body; (4) an intermediate sensual part that is shared with nonrational animals; and (5) an intelligence that is shared with the angels.

text: The essay says Pico is undecided in the Heptaplus about what the higher intellect illuminating ours is, God or a mind akin to man's, and does not identify it with the agent intellect.

quotes.text: He is less definite, though, about what this higher intellect is: “[a] greater, even divine, intellect illuminates the intellect in us, whether it be God (as some would have it) or a mind more nearly related to man’s, as almost all the Greeks and Arabs and many of the Hebrews hold.”

Following the medieval Arabic philosopher Alfarabi, Pico will call this higher intellect the “Spirit of the Lord,” but he stops short of identifying it as the “sun” of the Genesis creation story and the agent intellect of Aristotelian psychology.

open_questions.text: What the higher intellect is, God or a related mind, is left open by Pico's own phrasing.

basis_quote.text: He is less definite, though, about what this higher intellect is

judged.justification: Records that Pico leaves the identity of the illuminating intellect open.

text: The essay argues that Pico apparently entertained the Averroist unicity of the intellect, against Aquinas and against Ficino.

quotes.text: Against the grain of scholastic theologians like Aquinas as well as contemporary Florentine Platonists like Ficino, Pico apparently entertained the Averroistic doctrine of the unicity of intellect – that there is only one intellect for all human beings, and it is separate from all individuals.

warrants.text: The essay cites the thesis attributed to Averroes in the 900.

quote.text: he cites from Averroës the notorious thesis that “the intellective soul is one in all men.”

bears_on.note: the essay sets Pico's apparent entertaining of unicity against Ficino's position

judged.justification: Places Pico against Ficino on the unity of the intellect, a separate-substance question.

text: The essay judges that Pico's promise to reconcile Averroism with personal immortality remains unfulfilled, since a universal intellect cannot be reconciled with a personal soul.

quotes.text: Pico’s promise to reconcile Averroism, which lets personal immortality go, and Christianity, which holds on to it, remains unfulfilled, since the universal intellect of the former cannot be reconciled with the personal soul of the latter.

open_questions.text: In what sense a particular rational soul can be immortal if its intellectual part is fused with the whole separate intellect.

basis_quote.text: it remains very unclear in what sense a particular rational soul can be immortal

text: The essay's note says Pico reads the birth of Love from Plenty and Poverty in the Symposium as the growth of the Platonic Ideas in the Angelic Mind from an inchoate state to a perfected one through love.

quotes.text: Pico devotes Commento II.14–22 (trans. Jayne, 107–20) to an extensive interpretation of Plato’s Symposium 203B–C (the birth of love from the union of Plenty and Poverty) in terms of the growth of the Platonic Ideas in the Angelic Mind from an inchoate state (chaos) to a perfected one by means of love.

text: In a note the essay quotes the Commento for a first love that is in the Angelic Mind, called angelic or divine, and a second love in the rational soul, called human.

quotes.text: “[J]ust as the first love, which is in the Angelic Mind, is called angelic or divine, so the second love, which is in the Rational Soul, is called human love, because the rational faculty is the most important part of man’s nature”

text: The essay reads Pico's Oration as setting contemplation, associated with the cherubim, between the active life of the thrones and the unitive love of the seraphim, the highest order.

quotes.text: Contemplation, associated with the cherubim, thus belongs in the middle position between the active life of moral virtue, symbolized by the thrones, and the unitive perfection realized in perfected love, which belongs to the highest angelic order of seraphim.

warrants.text: The essay quotes Pico's passage on the seraph, cherub and throne.

quote.text: The seraph burns with the fire of charity; the cherub shines with the radiance of intelligence; the throne stands in steadfastness of judgment.

judged.justification: Maps the three orders onto three lives with the seraph highest.

text: The essay says the Dionysian triad of purification, illumination and perfection frames both the cherubic life Pico urges and the philosophical curriculum, and that the cherubim correspond most directly to illumination between the lower and higher orders.

quotes.text: The Dionysian triad of purification, illumination, and perfection is applied not only to frame the life of cherubim, which we are to emulate, but is also mapped onto the philosophical pedagogy that leads up to and beyond the limits of philosophy.
While the cherubim are described by Dionysius as being purified, illuminated, and perfected, they nonetheless correspond most directly with
illumination in relation to the lower and higher orders of angels, which represent purification and perfection, respectively.

judged.justification: Reads the Oration's philosophical stages through Dionysian angelology.

text: The essay reads Jacob's ladder in the Oration as a figure of nature, with descent and ascent standing for the analysis of the one into the many and the gathering of the many into one.

quotes.text: Pico appeals to the image of Jacob’s ladder to illustrate the relationship of the three orders of philosophy. As angels ascend and descend the many steps of the ladder, so must we, but the hands and feet that touch the ladder must first be washed “in moral philosophy as in living water.”

The ladder itself is a figure of nature, and the contrasting movements of descending and ascending refer, respectively, to the analysis of the one into the many and the gathering of the many into one.

text: The essay reads the midday light that inflames the Seraphim and illuminates the Cherubim as showing that natural philosophy does not suffice and that the highest illumination needs an infusion from beyond the soul.

quotes.text: This is that midday light, which, perpendicular, inflames the Seraphim, and at the same time illuminates the Cherubim.”

With this example, the distinction between natural and theological knowledge is underscored, since natural philosophy does not suffice to illuminate the soul. As in the example from Job, the movement upward to the highest reality requires an infusion from a source beyond the soul and the order of nature.

text: The essay observes that in On Being and the One Pico calls even angelic intellectual knowledge imperfect, in contrast to the Oration's emphasis on ascent, and it suggests the later works are perhaps more sober.

quotes.text: In On Being and the One, however, Pico points even to the imperfection of angelic knowledge, despite the fact that it requires no reasoning since it reaches its object directly:

While the Oration emphasized human freedom from a fixed nature, and the marvelous capacity to ascend the levels of being in knowledge, in his later, perhaps more sober, works, Pico emphasized instead the infirmity of human intelligence.

warrants.text: The essay quotes De ente et uno 5 (trans. Miller) on angelic knowledge.

quote.text: Even that [the intellectual knowledge of angels] is imperfect knowledge, at least because it seeks outside itself what it does not possess fully within itself, i.e., the light of truth which it lacks, and by which it is perfected.

judged.justification: Shows De ente et uno treating angelic knowledge as itself imperfect, which qualifies the Oration's ladder.

text: The essay argues that despite differences of context, the Oration and On Being and the One agree in doctrine that all knowledge remains imperfect until illuminated and united to its object, and that the seraphim too must undergo illumination.

quotes.text: there is a discernible consistency between them in philosophical doctrine. While the higher level of being and knowledge is perfect relative to the level just below it, all knowledge remains imperfect until it has been fully illuminated and united to its object. The imitation of the seraphim, which forms such a substantial part of the argument of the Oration, itself reminds us that they too must undergo an illumination in order to climb up to the height at which God dwells.

judged.justification: Offers a reading that reconciles the Oration with De ente et uno on angelic knowledge.

text: The essay says the Oration reminds the reader that love is ultimately higher than knowledge, since the seraphim are closer to God than the cherubim.

quotes.text: Pico reminds the reader that love is ultimately higher than knowledge, as the seraphim are closer to God than the cherubim.

text: The essay notes that Pico announces in the Oration and in the first of the theses according to his own opinion the theme that Aristotle and Plato agree in meaning and substance.

quotes.text: Pico announces this theme in the Oration and in the first of the 900 theses according to his own opinion: “There is no natural or divine question in which Aristotle and Plato do not agree in meaning and substance, although in their words they seem to disagree” (1>1)

text: The essay reports that the papal commission's list of thirteen theses included the thesis that it is more improper to say God is intellect than that the rational soul is an angel, and qualified it as wrong and open to a heretical twist.

quotes.text: The commission found thirteen theses that needed clarification and were in various degrees condemned.
12. It is more improperly said that God is intellect or that which has intellect, than that the rational soul is an angel. (3>49) Wrong and can be twisted to a heretical meaning.

warrants.text: The essay gives its own translation of the commission's judgments from Dorez and Thuasne (note 13).

quote.text: The commission’s judgments are my translation from Dorez and Thuasne, Pic de la Mirandole en France, 127–37.

bears_on.note: the commission's qualification of the thesis on the rational soul and the angel

judged.justification: Identifies the one angelological thesis on the commission's list and its qualification.

text: The essay hypothesizes that the members of the commission were those who had lobbied against Pico or that the pope wanted to chastise him, perhaps because of a tense political relationship with the Medici.

quotes.text: The fact that in the Breve that instituted the commission Innocent VIII equally referred to the judgment of “some learned people” without giving names allows the hypothesis that the members of the commission were those who had lobbied against the young scholar or that the pope himself wanted to chastise Pico. His motivation might have been a tense political relationship with the Medici of Florence, specifically Lorenzo

open_questions.text: The scholarly expertise of the commission's members and their interaction at the curia are unidentified.

basis_quote.text: Further interpretation of the commission and its motivation would depend on identifying the scholarly expertise of its members and their interaction at the papal curia.

bears_on.note: possible papal motive for the commission
Pico as Lorenzo's protege and the possible target of papal displeasure with the Medici

pico_locus.ref: first proem to second proem [Blum essay]

text: The essay says Pico's cosmology has three worlds, the transworldly (angelic or intellectual), the heavenly and the sublunary, which contain one another, so that the sun as fire in heaven is seraphic intellect in the transworld realm.

quotes.text: Pico’s cosmology starts with three layers of being, drawing upon the Platonic tradition: there are three worlds, the transworldly (or angelic or intellectual), the heavenly, and the sublunary worlds. The first is presided over by God, the middle one consists of the celestial spheres, and the third

consists of the inanimate and the living creatures. All these three worlds, however, are one, not only because they all stem from the same principle but, more importantly, because they contain each other mutually; what exists in the lower world also exists in the higher, only in a higher sense. For example, the sun is fire in the heaven, but in the transworld realm it is seraphic intellect.

warrants.text: Note 77 cites the Latin of the Heptaplus for the containment of the lower in the higher.

quote.text: Verum quae in mundo sunt inferiori, in superioribus sunt, sed meliore nota.

judged.justification: Gives the seraphic intellect as the transworld counterpart of the sun.

text: The essay argues that the Heptaplus turns what in the Oratio sounded like an appeal to man to find his place into an ontological-cosmological fourth world, and it allows that the Oratio perhaps was intended as such an appeal.

quotes.text: Now, in addition to this literally intricate cosmos, there is a fourth world, which is man, in whom again everything is contained that is in the others. Needless to say, this position resonates with Pico’s anthropology in his Oratio. Yet, the difference is also notable: what in the Oratio sounded like (and perhaps was intended to be) an appeal to man to find, if not determine, his proper place is now an ontological-cosmological hypostasis.

judged.justification: Reads the Oratio's dignity theme against the Heptaplus's cosmology.

text: The essay says that De ente et uno was presented on the surface as a polemical correction of Ficino's Platonism, but also defends the same view of God and his engagement in creatures as the Heptaplus.

quotes.text: On the surface, this booklet was presented as a polemical correction of Marsilio Ficino’s Platonism. But it also defends the same view of God and his engagement in creatures as seven times explained in Heptaplus, an engagement that piety is to emulate; God’s attributes are one in God “through simple, highest, ineffable, originative unity,” and consequently they are “above all things and outside all things, yet in such a way that not only are they very profound in all things, but are more one with all things than they are with themselves.”

bears_on.note: De ente et uno as a polemical correction of Ficino's Platonism, on the surface

judged.justification: Reads the dispute with Ficino as continuous with Heptaplus theology of divine attributes.

text: The essay says Pico denied the Neoplatonist doctrine that the One is separate from Being.

quotes.text: Pico denied the Neoplatonist doctrine that the One is separate from Being.

judged.justification: Compact statement of the disagreement with the Neoplatonists on the One.

text: The essay argues that De ente et uno closes with an exhortation to realize in life the convergence of the transcendentals, being, one, true and good, by returning to God, in whom they are identical.

quotes.text: it comes as no surprise that his last completed work, De ente et uno, closes with a similar message that exhorts readers to unify cognition and life toward God: “If these three, one, true, and good, follow by perpetual connection, it follows that when we are not these three, we absolutely are not, even though we may appear to be; and although we may be thought to live, yet we would be ever dying rather than living.”

The intention, however, is unmistakable, for it maintains that humans should realize the convergence of the transcendentals (being, one, true, good) – that is, the principles of cognition and the highest attributes of God – in their life by way of returning to God in whom these transcendentals are actually identical.

text: The essay reports that Pico hired the convert Flavius Mithridates to translate a corpus of Hebrew wisdom from which the Cabalistic parts of the 900 Theses were distilled.

quotes.text: While preparing for the great disputation, Pico hired the Jewish convert Flavius Mithridates (Raimundo Moncada) to translate a corpus of Hebrew wisdom, from which he would distill the Cabalistic parts of his 900 Theses.

bears_on.note: Mithridates translated the Hebrew corpus behind the Cabalistic theses

text: The essay says Pico's defence defines the Cabala as a second way of divine revelation, transmitted orally alongside the written law, and equates it with the anagogical sense of exegesis.

quotes.text: Cabala, however, is no such discipline; it is defined as a second way of divine revelation.

hidden under the shell [sub cortice] and raw face of the words.” That is, Moses received “a literal and a spiritual” law. Since God had forbidden the placement of the spiritual law into writing it was transmitted exclusively orally.
Pico points out that Cabala is equivalent to the sensus anagogicus of traditional biblical exegesis.

text: The essay says Pico refers to Maimonides as the one alleged to have first mentioned the old wisdom, that Maimonides became a Kabbalist through Mithridates's translations of Abulafia's commentary, and that Pico may have asked for them.

quotes.text: In explaining that the Church Fathers had only heard about that old wisdom, yet it was never diffused, he refers to Maimonides (“Rabbi Moyses de Aegypto”) who is alleged to have first mentioned it.

certainly Maimonides was “transformed into a Kabbalist” through Mithridates’ translations of Abrahm Abulafia’s commentary on Maimonides (Wirszubski, Pico della Mirandola’s Encounter, 84). Still, Pico may have asked him to do so.

hedge_words: may have asked him to do so

bears_on.note: Mithridates's translation of Abulafia on Maimonides as the route by which Maimonides became a Kabbalist

text: In a note the essay reports a disagreement about the Heptaplus and Cabala, one scholar seeking to absolve it of Cabalistic interests while another holds that Pico's interest in Cabala was unchanged until his death.

quotes.text: Di Napoli is eager to absolve the Heptaplus from Cabalistic interests (Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 284–5), whereas Garin maintains that Pico’s interest in Cabala remained unchanged until his death

open_questions.text: Whether the Heptaplus has Cabalistic interests, and whether Pico's interest in Cabala persisted to his death.

basis_quote.text: Di Napoli is eager to absolve the Heptaplus from Cabalistic interests

text: The essay says that around the time of the Heptaplus Pico endeavored to interpret the whole Bible, partly supported by Mithridates and Alemanno using the Hebrew sources they afforded.

quotes.text: he also endeavored to interpret the entire Bible, in part supported by Mithridates and Johanan Alemanno and using the Hebrew sources afforded by them.

bears_on.note: Mithridates as supplier of Hebrew sources

text: The essay names the major Kabbalistic works available to Pico and dates them: Sefer Yetsirah between the third and sixth centuries, the Bahir a twelfth-century compilation, and the Zohar probably of the thirteenth century.

quotes.text: The major works of Kabbalah available to Pico were Sefer Yetsirah (Book of Creation), written between the third and the sixth centuries; Sefer ha- Bahir (Book of Illumination), attributed to the Midrashic rabbi Nehunya ben ha-Kanah but in fact a twelfth-century compilation; and Zohar ([Book of] Splendor), attributed to the second-century mystic rabbi Simeon ben Yohai but probably written by Moses de Leon in the thirteenth century.

hedge_words: probably written by Moses de Leon

judged.justification: Supplies the datings needed to correct anachronistic source lists (audit A3 s6).

text: The essay says that when Pico wrote the Conclusions he also had commentaries by medieval Jewish authors, and that most of the works were translated for him by his teacher Mithridates.

quotes.text: When he wrote the Conclusions, Pico also had available to him works by medieval Jewish commentators such as Abraham Abulafia, Azriel ben Menahem of Gerona, and Menahem Recanati as well as several anonymous works. Most of the works were translated for Pico from the Hebrew by his teacher, Flavius Mithridates, a converted Jew and scholar of Kabbalah.

bears_on.note: Mithridates as Pico's teacher and translator of the Kabbalistic works

judged.justification: Lists the medieval commentators Pico could read, beyond the three main texts.

text: The essay says Mithridates annotated his translations and argued that Kabbalah proved the truth of Christianity, and that Pico presented Kabbalistic theses as strongly confirming the Christian religion.

quotes.text: Mithridates made marginal notations with his translation to guide his pupil and developed the argument that Kabbalah proved the truth of Christianity. Indeed, Pico claimed he was presenting Kabbalistic theses “strongly confirming the Christian religion using the Hebrew wisemen’s own principles.”

bears_on.note: Mithridates's Christian reading of Kabbalah, taken up by Pico

text: The essay reports Copenhaver's plausible argument that Kabbalah was central to the Conclusions and that even the number of theses had Kabbalistic significance.

quotes.text: From the perspective of Pico’s natural philosophy, his use of Kabbalah in the Conclusions was his most original and interesting contribution. In fact, Copenhaver has plausibly argued not only that Kabbalah was central to the Conclusions but that even the number of theses had Kabbalistic significance.

text: In a note the essay reports that Farmer and Copenhaver show that Pico was not indebted to Ficino for his ideas on magic and that the Hermetic corpus was a minor source for Pico, against the view that made Pico Ficino's disciple.

quotes.text: Frances Yates, Giordano Bruno, 84–116, suggested that the writings of Hermes Trismegistus were the critical source for Pico’s views on magic, as they had been for Ficino’s views, and that they made Pico into Ficino’s disciple, but as Farmer and Brian Copenhaver show, Pico was not indebted to Ficino for his ideas on magic, and the Hermetic corpus was a minor source for Pico.

bears_on.note: the note denies Pico's debt to Ficino for magic and reports Yates's contrary view

judged.justification: Qualifies the reading of Pico as Ficino's disciple in the matter of magic.

text: The essay says that against the astrological claim that heavenly bodies are agents of the deity, Pico posited angels, who mediate between us and God, as the agents governing human affairs.

quotes.text: but Pico denied the spiritual nature of the heavenly bodies. Against the astrological claim that the heavenly bodies were agents of the deity, Pico posited angels as those agents:

The sky was superior to the earth, according to Pico, but it was inferior to the human being, who had a rational soul. Only another being that possessed an intellectual nature could be superior to the human being or could act as an intermediary between the deity and the human being.

warrants.text: The essay quotes the Disputationes in translation.

quote.text: it is proper that human affairs be governed by the mystery not of bodies but of angels, who by nature and dignity mediate between us and God. So when you descend from God to the earth, you descend by means of the sky; when you descend from God to man, you descend by means of angels.

judged.justification: Shows the Disputationes using angels as the intermediaries between God and human affairs.

text: The essay argues that Pico made no direct reference to Kabbalah in the Disputations, and that his attack on the Kabbalists' recourse to the stars aimed at astrology and not at Kabbalistic study itself.

quotes.text: But Pico made no direct references to Kabbalah in the Disputations. He did note that “just as the astrologers contend that they find their images in the stars, so the Hebrew masters contend that they find their alef- beth, that is, the letters and elements of their language, in the stars.” This probably referred to the Kabbalists, but the attack was against their recourse to the stars, not Kabbalistic study itself.

open_questions.text: Whether Pico had set aside his Kabbalistic studies by the time of the Disputations.

basis_quote.text: Had Pico rejected Kabbalah by the time he wrote the Disputations? Had it ceased to exert an influence on him?

text: The essay suggests that Pico, without training in medicine or mathematics, may have been persuaded by Savonarola to give up his limited belief in astrology, unlike Ficino, who supported some level of astrology throughout his life.

quotes.text: Perhaps he was persuaded by the Dominican preacher Girolamo Savonarola to push his attack further than he had in his earlier works, as was first alleged by Lucas Bellanti in his defense of astrology written in 1497, the year after Pico’s Disputations was published.
Even Ficino, who was not as taken by Savonarola as his friend and supported some level of astrology throughout his life, may have been affected by the friar’s preaching on the subject

open_questions.text: What changed Pico's attitude to astrology; the sources are lacking.

basis_quote.text: What made Pico change his attitude toward astrology? Again, we lack the sources and must speculate.

bears_on.note: Savonarola's possible influence on Pico's attack on astrology
Ficino's differing position on astrology

text: The essay says Pico dedicated De ente et uno to Poliziano, asking indulgence for a technical vocabulary not yet fully at home in Latin and telling him not to look for stylistic embellishment.

quotes.text: Pico himself answered the question in the preface to his De ente et uno of 1491. Since this treatise dealt with complex issues of Aristotelian and Platonic metaphysics, Pico sought indulgence from Poliziano, to whom he dedicated the work, for employing a technical vocabulary “that was not yet perhaps fully at home in Latin” but was needed in order to express new concepts. Warning Poliziano not to look for the meretricious embellishment of an elegant style

bears_on.note: De ente et uno is dedicated to Poliziano, with a preface addressed to him on style

judged.justification: Establishes Poliziano as the dedicatee of De ente et uno, so the work was addressed to a humanist and not to Ficino.

text: The essay says Pico and Poliziano both regarded a highly worked style as unsuitable when the aim was instruction and not persuasion, and that Poliziano used the same Manilius quotation a year earlier.

quotes.text: Poliziano had used the same quotation from Manilius a year earlier in his Panepistemon, the academic prolusion to his 1490–1 course at the Florentine Studio on Aristotle’s Ethics, in order to make the same point
both Pico and Poliziano regarded a highly worked style as unsuitable when the aim was instruction, not persuasion.

bears_on.note: Pico and Poliziano shared the view that instruction does not require ornament

text: The essay says the papal commission had judged thirteen of Pico's theses heretical or of dubious orthodoxy, and that Pico adopted the Parisian style in the Apology as a deliberate provocation against its theologians.

quotes.text: Adopting the Parisian style mentioned by his scholastic for the theses was a pragmatic decision based on its centuries-long status as the lingua franca of philosophers. Adopting the same style in the Apology, however, was a deliberate act of provocation, directed against the theologians of the papal commission who had judged thirteen of his theses to be heretical or of dubious orthodoxy.

bears_on.note: Pico's stylistic provocation of the commission's theologians

text: The essay says Pico had used the idea that a text conceals hidden mysteries under its surface to interpret the Guide for the Perplexed, arguing that Maimonides embraces the mysteries of the Kabbalah in hidden insights.

quotes.text: Pico had also used this idea and its attendant metaphors to interpret the Guide for the Perplexed in his 900 Theses of 1486, arguing that while Maimonides “in the superficial bark of words appears to move with the philosophers, in the hidden insights of profound meaning he embraces the mysteries of the Kabbalah.”

text: The essay says Pico's method of concord between Plato and Aristotle distinguishes agreement in meaning and substance from apparent disagreement in words, and that he is preceded by Boethius, Augustine, Simplicius and Philoponus.

quotes.text: Pico’s comments regarding the first pair, Plato and Aristotle, are perhaps the best known, since they place him within a long tradition of commentators who contended that the greatest of Greek philosophers did not differ on the major points of their philosophies. As Pico notes, in his reconciliatory approach he is preceded by Boethius, Augustine, Simplicius, and John Philoponus.
contending that although in their words (verba) the philosophers may appear to be opposed, in meaning and substance (sensus et res) they are in accord.

judged.justification: Names the exegetical criterion, res over verba, that De ente et uno later applies.

pico_locus.ref: whole; dedicatory preface [Dougherty, Three Precursors essay]

text: The essay says that in De ente et uno Pico attempted to show the compatibility of the ultimate metaphysical commitments of Plato and Aristotle, and that his dedicatory preface announced a larger work on their concord.

quotes.text: Pico turned again to this issue of reconciling the two Greek philosophers in his late work, De ente et uno, in which he attempted to show the compatibility of the ultimate metaphysical commitments between Plato and Aristotle.
In the dedicatory preface to his De ente et uno, Pico noted his plans to write a larger work to be titled Concordia Platonis Aristotelisque.

quote.text: For a discussion of this reconciliation, see Michael J. B. Allen, “The Second Ficino-Pico Controversy: Parmenidean Poetry, Eristic, and the One,”

bears_on.note: the note directs the reader to the Ficino-Pico controversy over the One as the discussion of this reconciliation

judged.justification: Gives a concise statement of what De ente et uno set out to do and its planned sequel.

text: The essay reports one commentator's argument that Pico's claims of reconciliation are limited to three pairs of philosophers, so that a universalist theory of truth attributed to Pico is an overreading.

quotes.text: claims of reconciliation in the Oratio and the 900 Theses are limited to these three pairs of philosophers and has suggested that the tendency of some commentators to discover a purported reconciliation of all philosophers and philosophies is textually unwarranted.
See Craven, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 89–107, especially 97.

text: The essay suggests that Pico's more modest claims of reconciliation may be evidence that he held a stricter view of the ancient theology than Ficino.

quotes.text: Pico’s more modest claims in regard to reconciling the thoughts of certain pairs of philosophers may be evidence that Pico had a stricter view of prisca theologia than that of the Florentine master, Marsilio Ficino.

bears_on.note: a possible difference from Ficino on the extent of the ancient theology

judged.justification: Offers a contrast between Pico and Ficino on the scope of concord.

text: The essay reports that some commentators find Pico's views on the human condition to be influenced by contemporaries such as Ficino, and cites Kristeller for it.

quotes.text: Some commentators find Pico’s views on the human condition to be influenced by his philosophical contemporaries, such as the Florentine philosopher Marsilio Ficino.
See Kristeller, The Philosophy of Marsilio Ficino, 407–10.

bears_on.note: the reported view that Ficino influenced Pico's account of human nature

text: The essay reports that particular attention has been paid to Origen as a source for Pico's view of the human condition, especially Origen's contention that the human soul is a fallen angel.

quotes.text: Particular attention has been paid to the doctrines of Origen as an influential source for Pico’s views on the human condition, especially Origen’s contention the human soul is a fallen angel.

text: The essay says Pico sets out five options open to human beings, vegetative, sensitive, rational, angelic or divine lives, corresponding to plants, beasts, heavenly animals, angels and God.

quotes.text: Pico sets forth a fivefold range of options open to human beings, arguing that humans can seek to live vegetative, sensitive, rational, angelic, or divine lives, corresponding to the existing natures of plants, earthly beasts, heavenly animals, angels, and God.

pico_locus.ref: one spirit with God [Dougherty, Three Precursors essay]

text: The essay says Pico's notion of deification appears especially consonant with discussions in Pseudo-Dionysius and the wider Neoplatonic mystical tradition.

quotes.text: Here Pico invokes a notion of deification that appears especially consonant with discussions found in Pseudo-Dionysius as well as the general Neoplatonic mystical tradition.

judged.justification: Links the Oratio's deification to Dionysian mysticism, on Dougherty's reading.

text: The essay reports commentators who read Pico's use of Kabbalah as apologetic, corroborating Christian doctrine, against the view that he was interested in Kabbalistic texts in their own right, and notes that opinions differ on the sources themselves.

quotes.text: More recently, another commentator has argued against the celebrated view propounded by Frances Yates, that Pico was interested in magical and Kabbalistic texts in their own right. Instead, it is argued, Pico was governed by a strictly apologetic program in his approach to untraditional sources.

Even among those commentators who agree on the apologetic motivation underlying Pico’s forays into Hebrew sources, there is some disagreement on the tenor of Pico’s views regarding the sources themselves.

open_questions.text: Whether Pico's apologetic use of Kabbalah is compatible with valuing the sources themselves.

basis_quote.text: there is some disagreement on the tenor of Pico’s views regarding the sources themselves

text: The essay says copies of the 900 Theses circulated as far as Florence among Ficino's intellectual circle, though how widely they were available elsewhere is hard to discern.

quotes.text: Copies of the theses circulated as far as Florence among Marsilio Ficino’s intellectual circle, but it is difficult to discern how widely available the theses were to those in the farther reaches of Italy and Europe.

bears_on.note: the theses reached Ficino's circle

text: The essay says De ente et uno was dedicated to Poliziano, who had asked Pico to intervene in a dispute between the Platonists, Lorenzo and Ficino, and the Peripatetics, and that Pico seemed to disagree with the principles of the debate and used it to state his theories of concord.

quotes.text: In this same period, he also conceived and wrote De ente et uno, which circulated in Florence in manuscript form. This work was dedicated by Pico to his friend Poliziano, who had insistently asked him to intervene in

a dispute between the Platonists – in the persons of Lorenzo de’ Medici and Marsilio Ficino – and the Peripatetics or those who, like Poliziano, had always studied the texts of Aristotle. In reality, Pico seemed to disagree with the very principles of the debate and used the invitation as an occasion to articulate his theories on concord in public.

bears_on.note: Ficino, with Lorenzo, stands on the Platonist side of the dispute that occasioned De ente et uno
Poliziano, the Peripatetic-leaning dedicatee, insistently asked Pico to intervene
Lorenzo is named with Ficino on the Platonist side

judged.justification: Explains De ente et uno as an intervention in a Florentine dispute between Platonists and Peripatetics, with Pico rejecting the terms of the dispute.

text: The essay argues that the thesis of De ente et uno was not new, but Pico's reevaluation of the Parmenides, Sophist and Philebus and of Simplicius's commentaries was, as was his project to read Plato through Aristotle and medieval theologians as well as Plotinus and Proclus, which remained unpublished.

quotes.text: The question confronted in De ente et uno was not a new one for Pico, who had discussed it already with Elia del Medigo, among others. If the actual thesis of De ente et uno contained nothing new, certainly new was his reevaluation of the Parmenides, Sophist, and Philebus and Simplicius’s commentaries on Aristotle. His sophisticated project to read Plato not only through Plotinus and Proclus but also through Aristotle and medieval theologians also remained unpublished.

bears_on.note: the reevaluation of the Parmenides and Sophist and reading Plato via Aristotle stands against the Plotinus-and-Proclus reading of Ficino's school

judged.justification: Locates what was new in De ente et uno in the treatment of Plato's dialogues and Simplicius, not in the thesis.

pico_locus.ref: Avicenna and Averroes on the One [Borghesi essay]

text: The essay says Elia del Medigo joined Pico to discuss the theories of Avicenna and Averroes on the One, on Being and on Essence, after which Mithridates arrived.

quotes.text: As noted, following his passionate and dramatic adventure, Pico resumed his studies with increased commitment. Elia del Medigo joined him in order to discuss Avicenna’s and Averroës’s theories on the One, on Being, and on Essence. Soon Flavius Mithridates arrived in their midst as well.

bears_on.note: Mithridates arrives among Pico's teachers in the period of the Conclusiones

text: The essay reports that in 1484 Pico read Ficino's Theologia platonica, that Ficino later recalled Pico forcing him to tackle Plotinus, and that Pico assured friends he had not deserted the Aristotelian school.

quotes.text: In 1484, Pico read the Theologia platonica of Ficino, who later recalled how Pico, seized by enthusiasm, had forced him to tackle Plotinus shortly after he had published his translation of Plato. Nevertheless, Pico took the trouble to assure his friends that he had not deserted the Aristotelian school but was an explorer (explorator) of new territory who had not abandoned the ideas of the Ancients.

bears_on.note: Ficino's recollection of Pico urging him toward Plotinus

text: The essay says that in a letter of September 1486 Ficino asked Pico to return his Arabic Koran, and that Pico replied that he had not abandoned Plotinus, to whom Ficino apparently referred.

quotes.text: After a period of silence lasting until September of that year, a resumption in correspondence once again provides news of his activity. On September 8, 1486, Marsilio Ficino wrote to Pico, begging him to return his Arabic Koran.
As for Plotinus (to whom Ficino apparently referred), Pico vowed that he had not abandoned him and would continue to study his works.

bears_on.note: Ficino's letter of 8 September 1486 and Pico's reply, in which Plotinus is mentioned

text: The essay reports, from one of Ficino's letters, that Elia debated in Pico's house with the convert Mithridates, and says Mithridates soon began teaching Hebrew to Pico.

quotes.text: One of Ficino’s letters likewise informs us that Elia often held debates in Pico’s house on philosophical and religious matters with another converted Jew, Guglielmo Raimondo de Moncada, also known as Flavius Mithridates. The latter soon began teaching Hebrew to Pico, who was impatient to learn the language of the Bible.

bears_on.note: Mithridates as Pico's Hebrew teacher
Ficino is the report's source for the debates in Pico's house

text: The essay says Pico became the first Latin scholar to make explicit mention of the actual Cabala and has come to be considered the founder of the Christian Cabala.

quotes.text: He immersed himself particularly in the study of the Cabala, perfecting his knowledge to the point that he became the first Latin scholar to make explicit mention of the actual Cabala. In effect, he has come to be considered the founder of the Christian Cabala.

text: The introduction says Pico's Commento, ostensibly a commentary on a poem of Benivieni, examined Neoplatonic metaphysics and contained an implicit critique of the views of his friend Ficino.

quotes.text: His earliest philosophical work, the Commento, used the pretext of a commentary on a poem of Girolamo Benivieni (1453–1542) as an occasion for a philosophical examination of Neoplatonic metaphysics, and it contained an implicit critique of the views espoused by his friend, the great Florentine Neoplatonist philosopher and translator Marsilio Ficino (1433–99).

bears_on.note: an implicit critique of Ficino's views, between friends
the Commento is a commentary on Benivieni's poem

judged.justification: Frames the Commento as an implicit critique of Ficino, not only an exposition.

text: The introduction says De ente et uno was dedicated to Poliziano and resurrected the ancient thesis that Aristotle and Plato were not opposed on the relation between being and unity.

quotes.text: Pico’s brief metaphysical treatise, On Being and the One (De ente et uno), was dedicated to Angelo Poliziano (1454–94), a poet and scholar of the Medici circle. In this work, Pico discussed the question of the relationship of being and unity in light of the traditional Aristotelian and Platonic views, and he
resurrected the ancient thesis that Aristotle and Plato were not opposed on the question of the relation between being and unity.

bears_on.note: dedicatee of De ente et uno

text: The introduction says the Heptaplus was dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici and is a cosmological work in the form of a sevenfold commentary on the first portion of Genesis.

quotes.text: Pico’s Heptaplus, dedicated to Lorenzo de’ Medici (1449–92), was a cosmological work that took the form of a sevenfold commentary on the first portion of Genesis.

bears_on.note: the Heptaplus is dedicated to Lorenzo

text: The introduction says Pico's last works are most often seen in light of the influence of his close friend Savonarola, who clothed Pico in the Dominican habit and gave his funeral oration.

quotes.text: Pico’s last works, including short religious pieces and other biblical commentaries, are most often seen in light of the influence of Pico’s close friend in his later life, the fiery religious reformer Girolamo Savonarola (1452–98), who would ultimately clothe Pico in the habit of the Dominican order and give Pico’s funeral oration upon his untimely death.

bears_on.note: Savonarola as Pico's close friend in his later life
